items.title: Why telemetry was a mess  before  #databricks
items.content_snippet: In this NextGenLakehouse episode, I sit down with Robert (Bobby) Leach, a Senior Solutions Architect at Databricks, to trace observability from fragmented 1990s telemetry to today's open standard. We cover why "build a pipeline or pay Splunk/Datadog/New Relic" breaks at enterprise scale, how the 2019 merge of OpenCensus and OpenTracing created OpenTelemetry, and how Zerobus (part of Lakeflow Connect) now lands that telemetry directly in Unity Catalog. Full interview 👉 https://lnkd.in/eEdNJjYK

items.title: Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange
items.content_snippet: Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693). Amazon Cognito helps you add sign-up, sign-in, and access control to your web applications, mobile applications, and AI agents. With token exchange, a service or AI agent acting on a user's behalf can exchange the user's token for a new token scoped to a specific downstream service. items.title: Your Spec Has Bugs. Catch Them Before Your Agent Codes. - Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal, AWS
items.content_snippet: Spec-driven development only works if the spec is right, and specs are full of quiet bugs: rules that can't both hold, missing failure cases, sentences with two meanings. Your coding agent will faithfully build every one of them. Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal shows how Kiro catches these before any design or code is generated by pairing LLMs with SMT solvers, turning the model's own disagreement into a signal that a requirement is ambiguous. items.title: 225,000 Lines of Tests, Written and Merged by Agents - Kush Agrawal, Duolingo
items.content_snippet: Duolingo's iOS app has nearly 2 million lines of code, and its unit test coverage lagged far behind. Kush Agrawal walks through the autonomous pipeline that fixed it: scheduled workflows pick untested code, coding agents open pull requests, and a lifecycle manager monitors CI, fixes failures, runs AI review and merges, with engineers as the final reviewers. items.title: Agents Made Code Free. Maintaining It Didn't Get Cheaper. - Dmitry Buykin, Maersk
items.content_snippet: Coding agents made writing code almost free, but maintaining it didn't get any cheaper. Dmitry Buykin shares what happens months in, once agents write most of a large production codebase: tests that pass while production breaks, work nobody asked for, rules that contradict each other, and sprawl no one can review. He covers the patterns that actually help, from replaying real tasks and expert-owned evals to runtime guardrails and weekly pruning, and closes with an 18-question checklist for audit
